newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German growth outlook cut by key forecaster.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German growth outlook cut by key forecaster.

text.p: One of Germany's six leading economic institutes on Tuesday lowered its forecast for 1997 growth to two percent and said Germany was likely to miss the deficit target for European monetary union (EMU).
The Berlin-based DIW think-tank and its five peers had forecast as recently as October that 1997 growth in gross domestic product (GDP) would be 2.5 percent.
"The economic rebound of the past few years has been by far the weakest in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany," the DIW said in a report.
The DIW, closely affiliated with trade unions and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), also said it expected 1996 growth to be 1.5 percent, up from a November forecast of 1.25 percent.
That matches a Reuter poll of economists' forecasts for 1996 GDP which is scheduled to be released on Thursday.

Economists said growth virtually ground to a halt in the final quarter of 1996. The present cold weather could hamper construction so much that the economy might contract in the first quarter of 1997 -- as it did a year ago -- with little improvement likely before the spring, they said.

In its report, the DIW said Germany's budget deficit is likely to be about 3.4 percent of GDP this year, down from 3.9 percent of GDP last year but above the three percent target for inclusion in the planned single European currency.
Data for 1997 are crucial as they will be the basis for deciding which countries will participate in European monetary union (EMU) at the planned start in January 1999.
The institute also said German unemployment could climb to a record 4.5 million. Unemployment in November 1996 was 3.942 million before seasonal adjustment.
"The longer it takes to achieve a sweeping change in the labour market, the less likely is it that the government will meet its goal of halving unemployment by the year 2000," the report said.

Jobless data for December are also due for release on Thursday and analysts warn Germany faces a new unemployment blow with seasonally adjusted unemployment expected to rise between 35,000 and 60,000 from November's record 4.1 million.
Fear of losing one's job along with meagre wage rises agreed in major industries like the engineering sector, will keep consumers as reluctant as ever to open their wallets.
That will further hamper economic growth, economists say.
"Companies are incredibly sceptical, they are not convinced Germany has the preconditions for sustained growth," said Holger Fahrinkrug, an economist at UBS in Germany.
"There's a very big question mark over domestic demand and Germany cannot live from exports alone."
Ernst Schwanhold, economic policy spokesman for the SPD parliamentary faction, said the new DIW forecast proved it was time for a turnaround in economic policy.
Bonn should go on the offensive, together with its European neighbours, to stimulate jobs and growth, he said.

"The DIW is right to demand of German economic policy that instead of chasing after a reduction in the state share of the economy, that it improve its management of the economy and the social system," Schwanhold said.
"The currency union must be linked to a jobs (creation) union," he said.
DIW said the growth slowdown in formerly communist east Germany was the biggest cause for concern, predicting that the region's economy would stall in the second half of the year.
However, growth rates of four to five percent would be needed for the next several years for the east to reach a comparable level of prosperity with the west, it said.

But developments in the west have also been disappointing, DIW said. Since the end of the recession in 1993, the German economy has grown only 5.5 percent, far weaker than in the recovery of the early 1980s.
Domestic demand has not received the hoped-for boost from the export-driven recovery, it said.
